description: 1887 Jubilee Britain, ayahs and Lascars in London, Abdul Karim at court and the early South Asian diaspora.
content_html:
Why Context Matters for Drama Students

Understanding the social, cultural and historical context of a set play is not a separate academic exercise — it directly informs every staging and performance choice. When you know that the Lascar sailors had been settled in East London for generations by 1887, you can make a costume choice that reflects established community rather than recent arrival. When you know that Abdul Karim’s relationship with Victoria was a matter of documented record and court controversy, you can play the hostility of the English court as something felt, not invented. Context is the raw material from which staging decisions are made concrete and justified.

1887: The Golden Jubilee Year

The play opens in 1887, the year of Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee — the fiftieth anniversary of her accession. The Jubilee was a carefully managed spectacle of Imperial prestige: visiting dignitaries from across the Empire, public celebrations in London, military pageants. It was also the moment when Abdul Karim first arrived at Windsor as a young Indian man recruited to serve at the festivities. Gupta uses the Jubilee as a dramatic counterpoint: the public display of Imperial unity set against the private abandonment of women like Rani on the docks below.

For a designer, the Jubilee context opens specific aesthetic possibilities. Victorian royal ceremony had a known visual vocabulary: deep crimson and gold, military uniforms, gauze backdrops suggesting ceremonial grandeur. A director might use this vocabulary deliberately for the Windsor scenes and then undercut it: the same crimson and gold light that glamorises the Jubilee procession might, in a different scene, feel oppressive rather than celebratory when it falls on Abdul rather than on the English court.

Key Fact

1887 was the year of Victoria’s Golden Jubilee and the year Abdul Karim arrived at Windsor. Gupta uses the Jubilee as an ironic framing: the public spectacle of Empire at its height, set against the private abandonment of Rani at Tilbury Docks on the same day.

The British Raj and the Empress of India

Britain had ruled India directly since 1858, after the East India Company’s authority was dissolved following the uprising of 1857. Queen Victoria was formally declared Empress of India in 1876 — a title added at the suggestion of Benjamin Disraeli to make explicit the Imperial relationship. By 1887, India was the jewel of the Empire in official rhetoric: the source of enormous economic value, the proving ground for the British civil service, the largest territory under the Crown.

The practical human consequence of this relationship was a constant flow of Indian people into Britain: domestic servants accompanying colonial families on home leave, sailors recruited for British merchant shipping, traders and students, and eventually political figures such as Dadabhai Naoroji. The Empress stages the human texture of this flow — the real people whose arrival and often stranding in London the official Jubilee narrative had no place for.

The Ayahs and Their Home

The Ayahs’ Home in Hackney was a real institution: a hostel established by Christian missionaries to provide accommodation for Indian women stranded in London when the families they had travelled with could not or would not pay for their return. Gupta has placed the opening of the Ayahs’ Home slightly earlier than its actual documented date for dramatic compression. This is a standard technique in dramatic history: the playwright is not writing a documentary but using real institutions to give her invented characters authentic ground to stand on.

For a set designer, the Ayahs’ Home offers a richly specific environment: a Victorian terrace interior in Hackney, furnished with both English middle-class missionary taste (plain wooden furniture, Christian images) and the Indian domestic objects the women brought with them. The collision of these two aesthetics in the set dressing communicates the cultural in-between world the women inhabit — not fully at home in India because they are in England, not fully belonging to England because they are Indian.

The slight compression of the Ayahs’ Home timeline is a deliberate dramaturgical choice, not a historical error. Examiners expect students to demonstrate this understanding: Gupta is writing dramatic history, which means she shapes and compresses real events to serve the play’s dramatic and thematic needs. The play is not a history textbook and should not be judged as one. What matters is that the Ayahs’ Home was real, ayahs were really stranded in London, and the community that helped them was real — Gupta has brought these true facts onto the stage at the most dramatically compelling moment.

Lascar Sailors and the East London Community

The term “Lascar” referred broadly to Indian and South Asian sailors employed on British merchant ships. By the Victorian era, long-established Lascar communities existed in the dock districts of East London, particularly around Shadwell and the East India Dock. These communities had their own lodging houses, community networks and cultural practices. They were part of the city’s life, yet largely invisible to the official Victorian narrative of London.

As a designer staging the Lascar lodgings, the combination of maritime objects and South Asian domestic culture is the key to the scene’s atmosphere. Set design elements such as coiled rope, sea-chests, canvas and lanterns sit alongside cooking smells suggested by warm amber footlights and the sound of a Bengali folksong — a diegetic soundscape emanating from within the scene rather than externally applied.

Abdul Karim: The Historical Record

The historical Abdul Karim (c. 1863–1909) arrived at Windsor in June 1887. His relationship with Victoria is documented in her own diaries and in the diaries and letters of hostile courtiers. Victoria promoted him from personal attendant to Indian clerk to munshi; she asked to be taught Hindustani; she gave him a house and brought him to Scotland and the south of France on her travels. After her death in 1901, her son and heir Edward VII immediately had Abdul’s papers, diaries and letters burned and expelled him from Britain. The deliberate erasure of his record was itself a statement about whose history was permitted to exist.

Gupta stages this erasure as the play’s closing movement. For a lighting designer, the moment when Abdul’s world at court is systematically dismantled might use a slow fade to black for specific parts of the Windsor set while the rest of the stage remains lit — the physical erasure of his space mirroring the historical destruction of his papers.

Tanika Gupta and the RSC Commission

Tanika Gupta MBE was born in London in 1965 to parents of Bengali heritage. She has written extensively for the stage and television, and her work consistently returns to the experience of South Asian people within British history. The Empress was commissioned by the Royal Shakespeare Company for the Swan Theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, and premiered there in 2013 under the direction of Emma Rice. An RSC commission is a significant artistic statement: the institution most associated with Shakespeare’s canonical English cultural heritage choosing to stage a play that recovers the Indian presence within the British story. The RSC revival in 2023 at the Lyric Hammersmith, directed by Pooja Ghai, brought the play back into public view with a second major production.

Key Fact

The Empress was commissioned by the RSC and premiered at the Swan Theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, in 2013, directed by Emma Rice. The RSC’s commissioning choice was itself culturally significant: Gupta’s play brings the Indian presence in British history into the home of canonical British theatre.

Gupta is part of a tradition of Black and Asian British theatre-makers who have used the stage to recover histories excluded from mainstream cultural narrative. Her work shares ground with playwrights such as Winsome Pinnock, Roy Williams and Kwame Kwei-Armah, and with companies including the Tara Theatre and Tamasha, which have developed South Asian British theatre over several decades. Understanding this context helps students see The Empress not only as a history play but as an intervention in the question of whose history gets told on Britain’s major stages. The RSC commission brought that question to the most establishment of venues, with considerable dramaturgical intent.
exam_tip_html: For questions that ask about context, examiners do not want a list of historical facts — they want to see you applying context to specific staging decisions. Every contextual detail you raise should be followed immediately by its design or performance implication: “Because the Lascar community had been in East London for generations by 1887, a set designer might choose worn but carefully maintained domestic objects that signal established community rather than recent arrival — communicating permanence and belonging, which contrasts with Rani’s displacement.” For a 12-mark intentions question framed around context, show Gupta’s specific dramaturgical choice: why did she write this play for the RSC in 2013? What did she want a contemporary audience to understand about British history that the official narrative omits?
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The play is set in 1887, the year of Victoria’s Golden Jubilee, and draws on real institutions (the Ayahs’ Home, the Lascar community) and real people (Abdul Karim, loosely Dadabhai Naoroji) while using dramatic compression to serve the play’s theatrical needs.
  • Abdul Karim’s papers were burned after Victoria’s death — a historical erasure that Gupta stages as part of the play’s closing movement, using the production’s design vocabulary to make the destruction visible.
  • Gupta was commissioned by the RSC for the 2013 premiere; understanding the significance of that commissioning context helps students analyse her dramaturgical intentions for a contemporary audience.

practice_questions.text: In which year was Queen Victoria formally declared Empress of India?
What is a gauze in theatre design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a gauze is a fabric or material stretched across a stage space; 1 mark for explaining that it can create translucent or dissolving effects when lit from behind, used for backdrops or to suggest depth and distance (accept equivalent explanation).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a set designer could use the collision of English missionary furnishings and Indian domestic objects in the Ayahs' Home scenes to communicate the theme of cultural displacement.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of a specific English furnishing element (1) e.g. plain wooden mission-hall chairs or a Christian print on the wall; identification of a contrasting Indian object (1) e.g. a sari cloth folded on a chair, a brass cooking vessel or a child's toy from India; explanation of the contrast's effect on the audience (1) the cultural in-between world is made visible before a word is spoken; link to the theme of displacement (1) the women cannot fully belong to either world, and the set embodies that liminality.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Gupta uses the historical erasure of Abdul Karim's papers after Victoria's death as dramatic material. What staging choices could make this moment of erasure powerful for the audience?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the historical fact (Abdul's papers were burned by the royal household after Victoria's death in 1901) (1); identification of a specific staging choice for this moment (1) e.g. a slow fade to black on the Windsor set space while the rest of the stage remains lit; analysis of how this design choice makes historical destruction physically visible (1); link to Gupta's broader purpose: that the play itself is the recovery of a story that was deliberately destroyed (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse Gupta's intentions in choosing to set The Empress in 1887 — the year of the Golden Jubilee — and in staging the public spectacle of Empire alongside the private abandonment of Rani at the docks. What does she want the audience to think and feel about Victorian Britain?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12): Detailed analysis of at least three distinct intentions, each linked to a specific dramatic method: the Jubilee as ironic framing (Gupta wants the audience to feel the gap between official Imperial celebration and individual human cost); the choice to place Rani's abandonment in the same year as Abdul's arrival (the two characters are simultaneously products of the same Imperial system, one ascending and one discarded); the use of real institutions (the Ayahs' Home, the Lascar community) to give the play historical authority and make the audience feel they are being shown something true, not invented. Each intention linked to specific staging/dialogue/structural method and the intended audience effect. Substantiated judgement.

Secure (7–9): Two intentions clearly articulated with some reference to dramatic method and audience effect.

Developing (4–6): One intention identified; limited reference to method; audience effect implied.

Emerging (1–3): Describes the historical setting rather than analysing Gupta's dramaturgical purpose.

practice_questions.text: You are designing the production of The Empress for a large proscenium arch theatre. How would you use set design, lighting, sound and costume to communicate the contrast between the Golden Jubilee world of Windsor and the hidden world of the Lascar community and the Ayahs' Home to the audience? Refer to specific design choices for both worlds.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (17–20): Specific, justified choices across all four design disciplines applied to both worlds, with clear contrast between them. Windsor set design: raised levels, heavy drape or gauze backcloth in crimson and gold, a formal chair or dais for Victoria, sightlines that place the court in a hierarchy legible from every seat. Lascar/Ayahs' Home set design: lower, warmer space at stage level, maritime and domestic objects as props-as-symbols, no raised platform. Windsor lighting: deep gold and amber wash with a profile lantern special on Victoria's seat; profile lanterns for the court to create a sense of official illumination. East End lighting: warm low-level Fresnel wash, no specials, the suggestion of lamplight rather than stage light. Windsor sound: minimal, perhaps a formal orchestral underscore hinting at Victorian ceremony. East End sound: a diegetic soundscape with Bengali or Hindustani song from within the scene. Windsor costume: deep crimson and gilt for Victoria, black formal English tailoring for the court, Abdul's court livery marking him as different. Ayahs' Home costume: worn sari fabrics in blues and greens, suggesting the beauty of original garments after a long journey. All choices justified with reference to the historical context and the intended audience effect. Substantiated directorial judgement about how the contrast communicates the play's argument.

Secure (11–16): Most design areas covered for both worlds with concrete choices; contrast between the two worlds clearly established; effect on audience identified.

Developing (6–10): Some relevant choices but one or more areas missing or generic; contrast between worlds present but underdeveloped.

Emerging (1–5): Basic listing of choices with minimal justification; little sense of the designed contrast between worlds.

knowledge_checks.q: In which year was Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee, the year that opens The Empress?
What happened to Abdul Karim's papers after Queen Victoria's death?
options: They were donated to the Victoria and Albert Museum
They were returned to Abdul's family in India
They were stored in the Royal Archives at Windsor
They were burned by the royal household under Edward VII's orders

knowledge_checks.q: The Empress was commissioned by the RSC and premiered at the _____ Theatre in Stratford-upon-Avon in 2013.
Tanika Gupta placed the opening of the Ayahs' Home slightly earlier than its actual date as a form of _____ compression.
Match each historical figure or institution to the correct description:
right: Victoria's real Indian secretary whose papers were burned after her death
A real Hackney hostel for stranded Indian women, used by Gupta as setting
The first South Asian MP in British history, elected for Finsbury in 1892

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Golden Jubilee of 1887?
flashcard_questions.a: The 50th anniversary of Queen Victoria's reign, celebrated with Imperial spectacle in London.

flashcard_questions.q: When was Victoria declared Empress of India?
flashcard_questions.a: 1876, following a suggestion by Prime Minister Disraeli.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Ayahs' Home in Hackney?
flashcard_questions.a: A real hostel established by missionaries to house Indian women stranded in London.
Indian and South Asian sailors on British merchant ships, long settled in East London's dock districts.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to Abdul Karim's papers after Victoria died?
flashcard_questions.a: Edward VII had them burned and expelled Abdul from Britain immediately after her death.

flashcard_questions.q: Who directed the original 2013 RSC premiere of The Empress?
What is a gauze in theatre design?
flashcard_questions.a: A translucent fabric stretched across a stage, used for dissolving effects when lit from behind.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a fade to black?
flashcard_questions.a: A gradual reduction of lighting from a full state to complete darkness, closing a scene.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a diegetic sound in theatre?
flashcard_questions.a: Sound that comes from within the world of the play, as if the characters can hear it.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the RSC commissioning The Empress contextually significant?
flashcard_questions.a: The most canonical British theatre bringing an Indian-perspective history onto its stage was a cultural statement.
The overall visual environment a designer creates on stage to locate the action.
Shaping and condensing real events in time or sequence to serve a play's dramatic and thematic needs.

glossary_terms.definition: A fabric pulled taut across a stage space, used to create translucent backdrops, dissolving effects or the impression of depth and distance when lit from behind.
The overall visual environment of a production, encompassing the arrangement, materials, levels and style of everything the audience sees on stage.
Sound that originates within the world of the play, as if the characters can hear it, such as a song sung by a performer on stage or a knock at a door.
A gradual reduction of stage lighting from a full state to complete darkness, used to close a scene or the whole production.
The playwright's technique of shaping and condensing real events, timelines or sequences to serve the play's dramatic and thematic needs.
When a performer speaks directly to the audience, breaking the fourth wall to create a more immediate relationship between character and audience.
A lantern that produces a sharp-edged, focused beam of light; used for spotlights, gobos and precisely directed lighting effects.
